His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Destroyed were the companions of the trench﴾. That is, cursed. Ibn Abbas said: "Every instance of qutila (was destroyed) in the Quran means luʿina (was cursed)." This is the response to the oath, according to al-Farra', and the lam in it is implied, like His saying: ﴿By the sun and its brightness﴾ [al-Shams: 1], then He said: ﴿He has certainly succeeded who purifies it﴾ [al-Shams: 9], meaning, indeed he has succeeded. It was also said: there is inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, meaning, "Destroyed were the companions of the trench, and [by] the sky containing the constellations," as said by Abu Hatim al-Sijistani. Ibn al-Anbari said: this is an error, because it is not permissible for a speaker to say, "By God, Zayd stood," meaning "Zayd stood, by God." Some people said: the response to the oath is ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe﴾, and this is poor, because the speech has become long between the two. It was also said: ﴿Indeed, those who put to trial...﴾. It was also said: the response to the oath is omitted, meaning, "By the sky containing the constellations, you will certainly be resurrected." This is the choice of Ibn al-Anbari.

Al-Ukhdud (the trench) is a great split in the earth, elongated, like a ditch (khandaq); its plural is akhadid. From it comes al-khadd (the cheek), for the channels of tears, and al-mikhaddah (the pillow), because the cheek is placed upon it. It is said: takhaddada wajh al-rajul, when furrows of wounds have appeared on the man's face. Tarafa said:

"And a face as though the sun had draped its mantle over it, / Upon it a clear complexion, not furrowed."

﴿The fire containing the fuel﴾. "The fire" is a substitute for "the trench," a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). "Al-waqud," with a fatha on the waw, is the reading of the majority, and it means the firewood. Qatada, Abu Raja' and Nasr ibn Asim read it with a damma on the waw, as a verbal noun (masdar), meaning possessing blazing and flaring. It was also said: possessing the kindling of human bodies. Ashhab al-Uqaili, Abu al-Sammal al-Adawi and Ibn al-Sumayqa read "al-nar dhatu" with nominative case in both, meaning the fire containing the fuel burned them.

﴿When they were sitting over it﴾. That is, those who dug the trenches and sat over them, throwing the believers into them. They were in Najran, in the interval (fatra) between Jesus and Muhammad, may peace be upon them both. The narrators differed in their accounts, but the meaning is close. In Sahih Muslim, from Suhayb, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "There was a king among those before you, and he had a sorcerer. When the sorcerer grew old, he said to the king: 'I have grown old, so send me a boy whom I may teach sorcery.' So he sent him a boy to teach him. On his way, whenever he traveled, there was a monk, so he sat with him and heard his speech, and it pleased him. Whenever he came to the sorcerer he would sit with the monk, and when he came to the sorcerer he would be beaten. He complained of that to the monk, who said: 'When you fear the sorcerer, say: my family detained me. And when you fear your family, say: the sorcerer detained me.' While he was in that state, he came upon a great beast that had blocked the people, and he said: 'Today I will know whether the sorcerer is better or the monk is better.' He took a stone and said: 'O Allah, if the matter of the monk is more beloved to You than the matter of the sorcerer, then kill this beast, so that the people may pass.' He threw it and killed it, and the people passed. He came to the monk and informed him, and the monk said to him: 'My son, today you are better than me. Your matter has reached what I see, and you will be tested. If you are tested, do not point to me.' The boy used to heal the blind and the leper and treat people for all other ailments. A companion of the king who had become blind heard of him and brought him many gifts, saying: 'All of this is yours if you heal me.' He said: 'I do not heal anyone; it is Allah who heals. If you believe in Allah, I will invoke Allah and He will heal you?' So he believed in Allah, and Allah healed him. He came to the king and sat with him as he used to sit. The king said to him: 'Who restored your sight?' He said: 'My Lord.' He said: 'Do you have a lord other than me?' He said: 'My Lord and your Lord is Allah.' So the king seized him and continued to torture him until he pointed to the boy. The boy was brought, and the king said to him: 'My son! Has your sorcery reached the point that you heal the blind and the leper, and do this and that?' He said: 'I do not heal anyone; it is Allah who heals.' So the king seized him and continued to torture him until he pointed to the monk. The monk was brought, and it was said to him: 'Return from your religion.' He refused, so he called for a saw, placed the saw at the middle of his head, and split him until his two halves fell. Then the king's companion was brought, and it was said to him: 'Return from your religion.' He refused, so he placed the saw at the middle of his head and split him with it until his two halves fell. Then the boy was brought, and it was said to him: 'Return from your religion.' He refused, so the king handed him over to a group of his companions and said: 'Take him to such-and-such mountain, climb with him up the mountain, and when you reach its peak, if he returns from his religion, well and good; otherwise, throw him down.' They took him, climbed with him up the mountain, and he said: 'O Allah, suffice me against them however You will.' The mountain shook beneath them and they fell. He came walking to the king, and the king said to him: 'What has become of your companions?' He said: 'Allah has sufficed me against them.' So he handed him over to another group of his companions and said: 'Take him, carry him in a qurqur (a small boat), and bring him to the middle of the sea. If he returns from his religion, well and good; otherwise, cast him down.' They took him, and he said: 'O Allah, suffice me against them however You will.' The boat capsized with them, and they drowned. He came walking to the king, and the king said to him: 'What has become of your companions?' He said: 'Allah has sufficed me against them.' Then he said to the king: 'You will not kill me until you do what I command you.' He said: 'And what is it?' He said: 'Gather the people on one level plain, crucify me on a trunk, then take an arrow from my quiver, place the arrow in the belly of the bow, then say: In the name of Allah, Lord of the boy, then shoot me, for when you do that you will kill me.' So he gathered the people on one level plain, crucified him on a trunk, then took an arrow from his quiver, placed the arrow in the belly of the bow, then said: 'In the name of Allah, Lord of the boy,' and shot him. The arrow struck his temple, and he placed his hand on his temple at the place of the arrow, and died. The people said: 'We believe in the Lord of the boy! We believe in the Lord of the boy! We believe in the Lord of the boy!' The king was informed and it was said to him: 'Have you seen what you were fearing? By Allah, your fear has come upon you; the people have believed.' So he ordered the trench at the mouths of the lanes, and it was dug, and he kindled the fires and said: 'Whoever does not return from his religion, throw him into it'—or it was said to him, 'Plunge in'—and they did so, until a woman came with a child of hers, and she hesitated to fall into it, so the boy said to her: '(O mother, be patient, for you are upon the truth).'" Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it with its meaning. In it: "And on the boy's path there was a monk in a hermitage." Ma'mar said: "I think the people of the hermitages were Muslims at that time." And in it: "That the beast that blocked the people was a lion, and that the boy was buried"—he said—"it is mentioned that he was brought out in the time of Umar ibn al-Khattab with his finger on his temple just as he had placed it when he was killed." And he said: "A good, gharib hadith."

Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There was a king in Najran, and among his subjects was a man who had a young boy. He sent him to a sorcerer to teach him sorcery. The boy's path went by a monk who read the Injil, and what he heard from the monk pleased him, so he entered the monk's religion. One day he came upon a huge snake that had cut the people's path, so he took a stone and said: 'In the name of Allah, Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them,' and killed it." He mentioned something similar to what preceded. And when the king shot him with the arrow and killed him, the people of the king's realm said: "There is no god but the God of 'Abd Allah ibn Tha'mir," for that was the name of the boy. The king became angry and ordered trenches to be dug, wood and fire to be gathered in them, and he displayed the people of his realm before them: whoever turned back from monotheism he left alone, and whoever remained steadfast in his religion he threw into the fire. A nursing woman was brought, and it was said to her: "Return from your religion or we will throw you and your child." He said: she became fearful and was about to return, but the nursing infant said to her: "O my mother, remain steadfast in what you are upon, for this is only a brief moment," so they threw her and her son.

Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that the fire rose up from the trench and was forty cubits above the king and his companions, and it burned them.

Al-Dahhak said: "They were a people of the Christians who were in Yemen forty years before the mission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Yusuf ibn Sharahil ibn Tubba' al-Himyari seized them; they were more than eighty men, and he dug a trench for them and burned them in it." This was related by al-Mawardi. Al-Tha'labi related from him that the people of the trench were from the Children of Israel, who seized men and women, dug trenches for them, then kindled fire in them, then the believers were made to stand over it, and it was said to them: "Will you disbelieve or be thrown into the fire?" They claimed that they were Daniel and his companions, and this was said by Ata' al-Awfi. Something similar was related from Ibn Abbas. Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "A king became drunk and fell upon his sister, and he wanted to make that a law among his subjects, but they did not accept it. So she suggested that he preach that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had permitted marriage to sisters, but he was not heeded. So she suggested that he dig the trench for them and cast into it everyone who disobeyed him. He did so." He said: "And their remnants marry sisters, and they are the Magians, and they had been People of the Book." It was also related from Ali that the cause of the people of the trench was that a prophet whom Allah sent to Abyssinia was followed by some people, so their people dug a trench for them, and whoever followed the prophet was thrown into it. A woman was brought who had a nursing infant, and she was distressed, so he said to her: "O mother, go on and do not be distressed."

Abu Ayyub narrated from Ikrimah, who said: "'Destroyed were the companions of the trench': they were from your people, from Sijistan." Al-Kalbi said: "They were the Christians of Najran. They seized believing people, dug seven trenches for them, each trench forty cubits long and twelve cubits wide. Then naphtha was cast into it."

The fuel. Then they presented them to it, and whoever refused, they threw into it. It is said: they were a group of Christians in Constantinople at the time of Constantine. Muqatil said: the People of the Trench were three: one in Najran, another in al-Sham, and another in Fars. As for the one in al-Sham, he was Antiyanus the Roman; as for the one in Fars, he was Bukhtunassar; and the one in the land of the Arabs was Yusuf ibn Dhi Nuwas. God did not send down a Qur'an concerning the one in Fars and the one in al-Sham, but He sent down a Qur'an concerning the one in Najran. The reason was that two Muslim men, one of them in Tihama and the other in Najran, one of them hired himself out, and he began to work and to read the Gospel. The daughter of his employer saw light during the reading of the Gospel, so she informed her father, and he became Muslim. They numbered eighty-seven, men and women, after Jesus had been raised. Then Yusuf ibn Dhi Nuwas ibn Tubba' al-Himyari dug a trench for them, kindled fire in it, and presented them with disbelief. Whoever refused to disbelieve, he threw into the fire, and he said: whoever turns back from the religion of Jesus will not be thrown. A woman who had a small child who had not yet spoken turned back, and her son said to her: "O mother, I see before you a fire that will not be extinguished." So both of them threw themselves into the fire together, and God made her and her son to be in Paradise. On that single day seventy-seven people were thrown in.

Ibn Ishaq said, from Wahb ibn Munabbih: There was a man from the remnants of the people of the religion of Jesus son of Mary, peace be upon him, called Qimyun [in manuscripts A, H, W, and the History of al-Tabari: "Fimun" with a fa']. He was a righteous man, diligent, ascetic regarding the world, whose supplications were answered, and he wandered among the villages, never known in a village without leaving it. He was a builder who worked with clay. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: The people of Najran were idolaters who worshipped idols. In one of its villages near Najran there was a sorcerer who taught the boys of Najran sorcery. When Qimyun came to settle there, he built a tent between Najran and that village in which the sorcerer lived. The people of Najran began to send their boys to that sorcerer to teach them sorcery, so they sent 'Abd Allah ibn al-Thamir to him, and he was with the boys of Najran. Whenever 'Abd Allah passed by the owner of the tent, he was impressed by what he saw of his prayer and worship, so he began to sit with him and listen to him, until he became Muslim. He affirmed God's oneness and worshipped Him, and he began to ask him about the Greatest Name of God. The monk knew it, but he concealed it from him and said: "O nephew, you will not be able to bear it; I fear your weakness regarding it." Abu al-Thamir did not suppose anything except that his son was going to the sorcerer as the other boys did. When 'Abd Allah saw that the monk had been stingy with him in teaching the Greatest Name of God, he went to arrows [qidah (with kasra): an arrow before it is tipped and feathered; its plural is qidah], gathered them, and wrote on arrows every name of God that he knew, one name per arrow. When he had counted them, he kindled a fire for them, then began to throw them into it, arrow by arrow, until when he came to the Greatest Name he threw his arrow into it, and the arrow leapt and came out of it, nothing harming it. He took it and went to his companion and informed him that he had learned the Greatest Name of God which he had concealed from him. He said: "What is it?" He said: "Such and such." He said: "How did you learn it?" So he told him what he had done. The monk said: "O nephew, you have hit upon it; keep it to yourself, and I do not think you will do so." Then whenever 'Abd Allah ibn al-Thamir entered Najran, he would not meet anyone afflicted with harm without saying: "O 'Abd Allah, will you affirm God's oneness and enter my religion, so that I may supplicate God for you and He will heal you from what you are in of affliction?" He would say: "Yes," and he would affirm God's oneness and submit, and he would supplicate God for him and he would be healed. Until no one in Najran remained who was afflicted with harm without coming to him, following his religion, and he supplicated for him and he was healed. Until his affair was reported to their king, who summoned him and said to him: "You have corrupted the people of my town and opposed my religion and the religion of my fathers, so I will surely make an example of you." He said: "You cannot do that." So he began to send him up a high mountain, from which he was cast down from its top, and he fell to the ground with no harm to him. He began to send him to the waters of Najran, seas into which nothing thrown is spared, and he was thrown in and came out with no harm to him. When he overcame him, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Thamir said to him: "By God, you will not be able to kill me until you affirm God's oneness and believe in what I have believed in; for if you do that, you will be empowered over me and will kill me." So that king affirmed God's oneness and bore witness to his testimony. Then he struck him with a staff, wounding him with a small wound, not a large one, and he died. The king died in his place, and the people of Najran gathered upon the religion of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Thamir, which was in accordance with what Jesus son of Mary had brought of the Gospel and its law. Then what had befallen the people of their religion of new events befell them, and from this came the origin of Christianity in Najran. Then Dhu Nuwas the Jew advanced against them with his armies from Himyar, invited them to Judaism, and gave them the choice between that and death. They chose death, so he dug the trench for them, burning them with fire and killing them with the sword, and mutilating them, until he had killed twenty thousand of them. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: twelve thousand. Al-Kalbi said: the People of the Trench were seventy [in manuscripts Z and L: "ninety"] thousand.

Wahb said: Then, when Aryat overcame Yemen, Dhu Nuwas fled, plunged into the sea on his horse, and drowned. Ibn Ishaq said: This Dhu Nuwas, his name was Zur'a ibn Tubban As'ad al-Himyari, and he was also called Yusuf. He had braids of hair that swayed, that is, they moved about, so he was named Dhu Nuwas. He did this to the people of Najran. A man named Dawas Dhu Tha'laban escaped from them, and he led the Abyssinians to seek support through them, so they took possession of Yemen. Dhu Nuwas perished in the sea, having cast himself into it. In regard to him 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib said:

Do you threaten me as if you were Dhu Ru'ayn [in the finest of life] or Dhu Nuwas?
How many before you possessed blessings and an enduring kingdom among people, firm.
Its covenant is ancient, from the time of 'Ad, the great, the conqueror, the tyrannical, the harsh.
Time removed their kingdom, and it became transferred from people to people.

Dhu Ru'ayn: a king of the kings of Himyar. Ru'ayn is a fortress belonging to him, and he is of the descendants of al-Harith ibn 'Amr ibn Himyar ibn Saba'.

Issue: Our scholars said: In this verse God informed the believers of this community of what those who affirmed God's oneness before them faced of hardships, consoling them with that. The Prophet (ﷺ) also related to them the story of the boy so that they might endure what they encounter of harm and pains and the hardships in which they were, in order to take as their model such a boy, in his patience, his steadfastness in truth, his adherence to it, and his giving up of his soul for the sake of making his call manifest, and people entering the religion despite his young age and the greatness of his patience. Likewise the monk endured holding fast to the truth until he was sawn in two with a saw. Likewise many people, when they believed in God the Exalted and faith took root in their hearts, endured being thrown into the fire and did not turn back in their religion. Ibn al-'Arabi said: This is abrogated (mansukh) according to us, as its explanation was already given in Surah al-Nahl. [See vol. 10, p. 180 and p. 202.] I say: It is not abrogated according to us, and enduring that is more excellent for one whose soul is strong and whose religion is firm. God the Exalted said, reporting about Luqman: ﴿O my son, establish the prayer, enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and bear patiently what befalls you; indeed, that is of the matters requiring resolve﴾ [Luqman 31:17]. [See vol. 14, p. 68.] Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Among the greatest jihad is a word of justice before an oppressive ruler." It was recorded by al-Tirmidhi, who said: a hasan gharib hadith. Ibn Sinjar (Muhammad ibn Sinjar) narrated from Umayma, a freed slave-woman of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: I was pouring water for the Prophet (ﷺ) for ablution when a man came and said: "Advise me." He said: "Do not associate anything with God, even if you are cut to pieces or burned with fire..." [the hadith in full]. Our scholars said: Many of the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) were tested with killing, crucifixion, and severe torture, yet they endured and paid no attention to any of that. The story of 'Asim, Khubayb, and their companions suffices you, and what they met of wars, trials, killing, captivity, burning, and other things. It has already passed in Surah al-Nahl that this is a consensus (ijma') of those who were strong in that; so reflect on it there. [See vol. 10, p. 180.]

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Cursed be the companions of the trench﴾. This is an invocation against these disbelievers, that they be removed from God's mercy. It is said: its meaning is a report about the killing of those believers, that is, they were killed by fire and they endured. It is also said: it is a report about those wrongdoers; it is narrated that God took the souls of those who were thrown into the trench before they reached the fire, and a fire came out of the trench and burned those who were sitting around it. It is also said: the believers were saved, and the fire burned those who sat, as al-Nahhas mentioned. The meaning of ﴿upon it﴾ is "before it"; 'ala here means 'inda ("beside"). It is also said: 'alayha means "over what draws near to it from the edges of the trench," as the poet said:

And the dew and the one who shaves [his head] spent the night over the fire [of the gatherers]. [The line is by A'sha Qays, its first half being: "They flare up for the two chilled ones who warm themselves by it."]

The governing element of ﴿when﴾ is "cursed": that is, they were cursed at that time.

﴿And they, over what they were doing to the believers, were witnesses﴾: that is, present. It means the disbelievers, who would present disbelief to the believers, and whoever refused they would throw into the fire. In this He described them with cruelty and with zeal in that. [In some copies: "that is, with the eternal (al-khuld)" instead of "then with zeal (al-jadd)".] It is also said: 'ala here means ma'a ("with"), that is: and they, along with what they were doing to the believers, were witnesses.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they did not hold it against them﴾. Abu Haywa read (naqimu) with a kasra, but the eloquent (fasih) reading is with a fatha, and the discussion of it has already passed in (Bara'a) [[See vol. 8, p. 207.]]: that is, the king and his companions did not hold it against those whom they burned, ﴿except that they believed﴾, that is, except that they affirmed, ﴿in Allah, the Almighty﴾, that is, the Dominant, the Impregnable.

﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, that is, the One praised in every state.

﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, with no partner in them and no equal, ﴿and Allah is over all things a Witness﴾, that is, Knowing of the deeds of His creation, nothing hidden from Him is concealed.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And they did not hold it against them﴾. Abu Haywa read (naqimu) with a kasra, but the eloquent (fasih) reading is with a fatha, and the discussion of it has already passed in (Bara'a) [[See vol. 8, p. 207.]]: that is, the king and his companions did not hold it against those whom they burned, ﴿except that they believed﴾, that is, except that they affirmed, ﴿in Allah, the Almighty﴾, that is, the Dominant, the Impregnable.

﴿the Praiseworthy﴾, that is, the One praised in every state.

﴿to whom belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, with no partner in them and no equal, ﴿and Allah is over all things a Witness﴾, that is, Knowing of the deeds of His creation, nothing hidden from Him is concealed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 85, verse 10–11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who persecuted the believing men and believing women﴾ means: they burned them with fire. The Arabs say: "So-and-so tested (fatana) the dirham and the dinar," when he put it into the furnace (al-kawr) to examine its quality. A dinar is then called maftun (tested). The goldsmith is called al-fattan (the one who tests), and likewise the Shaytan. Waraq fatin means molten silver (fiddah muhtariqah). The harra (lava field) (with a fatha on the ha', an unplanted land of black, porous stones) is called fatin, as if its stones had been burned by fire, owing to their blackness.

(Then they did not repent) means: from their foul deed, despite the signs and clear proofs that Allah had manifested to this tyrant, oppressive king and his people through the youth.

(Then for them is the punishment of Hell) because of their disbelief.

(And for them is the punishment of the Burning) in this world, because they burned the believers with fire. This has already been related from Ibn 'Abbas. It has also been said: ﴿And for them is the punishment of the Burning﴾ means: for them in the Hereafter is a punishment in addition to the punishment of their disbelief, because of what they did to the believers by burning them. It has also been said: for them is a punishment, and the punishment of Hell is the Burning. Al-Harid (the Burning) is one of the names of Hell, like al-Sa'ir (the Blaze). Hell has levels (darakat), types, and names. It is said that they are punished with al-zamharir (extreme cold) in Hell, and then they are punished with the punishment of the Burning. The first is punishment by its cold, and the second is punishment by its heat.

(Indeed, those who believed) means: those who had believed in Allah, that is, affirmed Him and His messengers.

(And did righteous deeds, for them are gardens) means: orchards.

(Beneath which rivers flow) of water that does not change, and of milk whose taste has not altered, and of wine delightful to those who drink it, and rivers of clarified honey.

(That is the great triumph) means: the magnificent one, for which there is no triumph comparable, and nothing resembles it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 85, verse 12–16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord is severe.﴾ That is, His seizing of the tyrants (jababira) and the wrongdoers (zalama), like His saying, the One whose praise is exalted: ﴿And thus is the seizure of your Lord when He seizes the cities while they are wrongdoing. Indeed, His seizure is painful and severe.﴾ [Hud: 102]. This has already been discussed [see vol. 9, p. 95].

Al-Mubarrad said: ﴿Indeed, the seizure of your Lord﴾ is the answer to the oath. The meaning is: "By the sky containing the constellations, indeed the seizure of your Lord..." and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion emphasizing the oath. It was said: it is the Mother of the Book (*Umm al-Kitab*), and from it the Qur'an and the other scriptures were copied. Al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*) is of red ruby. Its top is attached to the Throne and its bottom is in the lap of an angel called Matiriyun [[In Ruh al-Ma'ani: (Satarbun).]]. Its writing is light and its pen is light. Allah the Mighty and Majestic looks into it three hundred and sixty times each day. There is no glance but that He does what He wills: He raises the lowly, lowers the exalted, enriches the poor, impoverishes the rich, gives life and causes death, and does what He wills. There is no god but Him." Anas ibn Malik and Mujahid said: the Preserved Tablet which Allah mentioned is on the forehead of Israfil. Muqatil said: the Preserved Tablet is to the right of the Throne. It was also said: the Preserved Tablet is that in which are the kinds of creation and their creation, the clarification of their affairs, the mention of their terms, their provisions and their deeds, the decrees executed concerning them, and the final outcome of their affairs; and it is the Mother of the Book. Ibn Abbas said: "The first thing Allah the Exalted wrote in the Preserved Tablet was: 'Indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but I. Muhammad is My messenger. Whoever submits to My decree, endures My trial, and gives thanks for My blessings, I shall record him as a truthful one (*siddiq*) and raise him among the truthful.
